planting.note: Transplant young container-grown trees (ideally under 80 cm tall) in spring, since larger lenga beeches resent root disturbance and their fine roots dry out quickly if exposed; choose a site with cool, moist, lime-free soil and full sun.

directions: Lenga beech is a cold-hardy deciduous Nothofagus from the timberline forests of Tierra del Fuego and the southern Andes, where it forms the southernmost broadleaf forests on Earth. Its small, rounded leaves turn vivid orange and red before falling in autumn, a striking departure from the evergreen character of most Patagonian forest trees. It thrives in cool, humid, maritime climates with consistent moisture and resents both summer heat and limy soils. Because young trees have very fine, drought-sensitive roots, nursery stock should be planted while still small and watered closely through its first seasons.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in a site sheltered from cold, drying winds, since this evergreen beech will not tolerate exposure despite tolerating damp, mild winters; choose full sun and humus-rich, lime-free soil.

directions: Magellan's beech is an evergreen Nothofagus from the wet forests of Tierra del Fuego and southern Chile, where it grows alongside lenga and coigüe in some of the coolest broadleaf forest on Earth. Its small, dark, toothed leaves stay on the tree year-round, giving it a yew-like density unusual among southern beeches. It was the first Nothofagus species widely grown in Britain and Ireland, valued for tolerating damp, mild winters, though it grows markedly slower in cultivation than in its native range and dislikes both cold wind and chalky soil. Give it full sun and a sheltered, humid site with consistently moist, acidic soil.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown firebush in spring once frost danger has passed, in a sheltered, sunny site with acidic, well-drained, lean soil; avoid rich manured ground, which encourages soft growth that is more frost-tender.

directions: Chilean firebush, known locally as notro, is an evergreen to semi-evergreen tree of the Valdivian and Magellanic forest margins of Chile and Argentina, prized for the brilliant tubular scarlet-to-orange flowers that smother its branches in late spring and early summer. The narrow, leathery leaves are a useful foil for the intense flower color, and the species often suckers from the base, forming a thicket if not controlled. It requires acidic, well-drained soil and resents both lime and rich, manured ground, which weakens frost hardiness. In cold climates it is often grown against a warm wall or given winter protection while young, since hardiness varies considerably between seed-grown individuals.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant young container-grown trees in spring on a sheltered, humid site such as a woodland edge or north-facing slope, in moist but free-draining acidic soil; growth is extremely slow, so choose a permanent position from the start.

directions: Alerce, or Patagonian cypress, is a scale-leaved conifer from the wet temperate forests of southern Chile and Argentina, where ancient individuals rank among the longest-lived trees on Earth, rivaling the bristlecone pines of North America in age. In cultivation it remains a rare, slow-growing specialist tree, thriving only in consistently humid, mild, maritime climates such as those of the British Isles, Ireland, and the Pacific Northwest. It dislikes both summer drought and cold, drying winds, performing best with the shelter of a woodland edge or north-facing slope. Because of its extreme longevity and slow growth rate, it is grown chiefly by conifer collectors and specialist arboreta rather than for quick garden impact.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in consistently moist, acidic soil; this wind- and salt-tolerant evergreen is well suited to exposed coastal or maritime gardens where many other broadleaf evergreens struggle.

directions: Magellan's mayten is a small evergreen tree or large shrub from the subantarctic forests of Tierra del Fuego and the Chilean and Argentine Magellanic region, where it grows alongside lenga and coigüe beeches. Its toothed, glossy leaves surround small, inconspicuous flowers that carry a surprising orange-blossom scent in spring. Unlike many forest-margin natives of this region, it tolerates wind and salt spray well, making it useful in exposed coastal gardens from the British Isles to the Pacific Northwest. It performs best with cool summers and struggles in prolonged heat and humidity, needing evenly moist, acidic soil to thrive.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Sow seed in pots in autumn and leave in a cold frame over winter, since cold, moist stratification is required for germination; transplant seedlings to a permanently moist, humus-rich site the following spring.

directions: Native to wet alpine meadows and streamsides above the treeline from eastern Turkey through the Caucasus, this primrose grows where snowmelt keeps the ground constantly saturated through the growing season. Its rose-pink to lilac flowers, each with a paler eye, open in rounded clusters held well above a rosette of toothed leaves in late spring. Because it comes from permanently wet montane ground, it fails quickly in soil that dries out even briefly, and is best grown in a bog garden, streamside bed, or heavily irrigated alpine bed. Light shade from the heat of the day helps it persist through summer outside its native cool, humid highlands.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in autumn directly where it is to grow or in deep pots, since the long taproot resents transplanting; seedlings establish over winter and flower from their second spring.

directions: Golden pasque flower is a high-alpine buttercup relative from open, grassy meadows and light woodland in the Georgian Caucasus and adjacent northeastern Turkey, growing above where most competing vegetation thins out. In mid-to-late spring it sends up large, silky, deep golden-yellow bells covered in fine silvery hair, opening later in the season than most other pasque flowers. Like its relatives, it carries a long, woody taproot that resents disturbance, so seed should be sown where the plant is to stay, or in deep pots for later planting out while still young. Give it gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid winter wet, which is far more damaging to this species than cold.

planting.note: Direct sow seed outdoors in autumn, since this poppy establishes readily from seed and spreads gently by creeping underground roots once settled; choose a sunny, well-drained rocky or gravelly site.

directions: Armenian poppy is a long-lived perennial poppy from the rocky highlands of Armenia and the eastern Caucasus, distinguished from most poppies by spreading gently through underground runners rather than staying as a single clump. Pale buds unfurl into light orange, semi-double flowers held above neatly toothed, hairy foliage from late spring into early summer. It thrives in the dry, stony crevices of a rock garden or scree bed, including soils with chalk or limestone, and resents heavy, waterlogged ground far more than it minds drought or cold. Deadheading extends bloom, and established plants slowly widen into a loose patch rather than seeding aggressively.

planting.note: Plant small, nursery-grown rosettes in spring into a gritty, humus-poor mix in a trough, raised bed, or rock garden crevice, since this slow cushion-forming saxifrage resists overly rich or wet ground.

directions: Juniper-leaf saxifrage forms a tight, spiny-looking cushion of dark green, needle-tipped rosettes native to damp limestone rocks and cliffs in the alpine zone of the Caucasus. In early spring, short stalks lift clusters of bright yellow flowers just above the foliage for a few weeks before the plant returns to its quiet cushion form for the rest of the year. It is a true alpine specialist, needing gritty, sharply drained soil, cool roots, and protection from standing winter wet, conditions most easily provided in a trough, raised bed, or alpine house. Because it remains uncommon in general cultivation, plants or seed are generally sourced through specialist alpine nurseries or society seed exchanges.

planting.note: Transplant young plants in spring into a sunny rock crevice, raised bed, or trough with sharply drained, lean soil; in hot-summer gardens give it morning sun and afternoon shade to mimic its cool mountain home.

directions: Three-toothed bellflower is a diminutive rock-crevice perennial from high elevations of the Transcaucasus and adjoining northeastern Turkey, where it roots into bare stone between 1,800 and 3,400 meters. Each short stem carries one or a few bicolor bell-shaped flowers, blue to violet with a conspicuous white base, over a low mat of foliage in summer. It wants sharp drainage above all else, since winter wet is far more likely to kill it than cold, and performs best in a raised bed, wall crevice, or alpine trough filled with lean, gritty soil. In regions with hot summers, afternoon shade and a cool root zone help it persist season to season rather than behaving as a short-lived annual.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or transplant nursery-grown plants in spring into full sun and moist but well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil.

directions: Blood pink is a semi-evergreen Dianthus from dry, sunny slopes of the Transcaucasus, Turkey, and Iran, named for its intensely saturated blood-red flowers, a shade unusual among wild pinks that tend toward softer rose tones. Tight, rounded flower heads cluster atop slender stems above grassy, blue-green foliage from early to late summer, carrying a light clove scent. Unlike many dianthus adapted to lean, gritty ground, this species prefers soil that is evenly moist but still free-draining, and resents being waterlogged over winter. Trim plants back after the first flush of bloom to tidy the foliage and encourage a second round of flowers later in the season.

planting.note: Plant young nursery-grown plants in spring into full sun, in sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil such as a rock garden, raised bed, or trough; good winter drainage matters far more to survival than cold.

directions: Caucasus skullcap is a low, woody-based, creeping perennial found on gravelly, limestone-rich slopes from the Caucasus Mountains of Georgia and Russia west to Greece and Turkey. From late spring through summer it produces hooded, tubular, bright yellow flowers, sometimes flushed with red on the lower lip, held just above a mat of small gray-green leaves. It is markedly drought-tolerant once established and prefers alkaline to neutral, sharply drained soil, making it a good match for a sunny rock garden, wall, or large trough. Excess winter moisture is its main vulnerability, so raised or sloped plantings that shed water quickly suit it far better than flat, heavy ground.
